reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Timber Piles
sections.summary: Pile toe attachments and splice accessories ease installation, reduce damage and suit heavy loads, sloping rock, obstructions and long piles, but add cost and should be used only when needed; they must develop the required structural resistance in driving and service. Timber piles risk toe and head splitting and brooming, body splitting or bowing, and breakage.
sections.body: 16.1 Timber Piles (p. 395). Chapter intro: accessories protect pile toes or facilitate splicing; they can make installation easier and faster, reduce damage and give more dependable support; heavier loads, sloping rock, obstructions and longer piles often make toe attachments and splices cost effective or necessary, but they add significant cost and should not be used unless needed. Toe attachments and splices for timber, steel, concrete and composite piles are covered; during driving and under all loadings they should develop the required structural resistance. Timber piles: problems include splitting and brooming of the toe and/or head, splitting or bowing of the body, and breaking during driving; protective attachments at toe and head minimize them (16.1.1 to 16.1.3).
key_points: Use toe attachments and splices only where needed; they add significant cost
Accessories must develop the required structural resistance in driving and service
Timber pile problems: toe/head splitting and brooming, body splitting or bowing, breakage
sections.applicability: Toe protection, head banding and splicing of timber piles.

sections.title: Pile Toe Attachments
sections.summary: Timber pile toes are protected by steel boots (cover the whole toe without trimming) or points (toe trimmed to fit), both quickly fixed with nailed straps; larger hammers and higher resistances raise the risk of damage at obstructions.
sections.body: 16.1.1 Pile Toe Attachments (pp. 395 to 396). Timber toe protection uses steel boots or points; larger hammers and higher nominal resistances raise the damage risk if obstructions are met. Boots cover the entire toe without trimming; points require trimming the toe to fit (Figure 16-1). Both are secured quickly in the field by nailing the shoe straps to the toe (the printed sentence on fitting is garbled). Figure 16-2 shows a boot attached.
key_points: Steel boots cover the entire toe without trimming; points need the toe trimmed
Both attach quickly by nailing shoe straps to the toe

figures.title: Timber pile toe attachments: (a) Pile boot and (b) Pile point
Timber pile with pile boot attached

sections.applicability: Toe protection for timber piles.

sections.title: Attachments at Pile Head
sections.summary: Band timber pile heads with heavy metal strapping before driving to prevent splitting; AASHTO (2010) requires collars, bands or other devices when the required nominal driving resistance exceeds 200 kips.
sections.body: 16.1.2 Attachments at Pile Head (p. 397). The American Wood Preservers Institute (cited as Collin 2012; the reference list prints Collin 2002) recommends banding timber pile heads with heavy metal strapping before driving to prevent splitting. AASHTO (2010) requires collars, bands or other devices against splitting and brooming when the required nominal driving resistance on a timber pile exceeds 200 kips (Figure 16-3).
key_points: Band timber pile heads with heavy metal strapping before driving
AASHTO (2010): collars or bands required above 200 kips nominal driving resistance

figures.title: Banded timber pile head

sections.applicability: Head protection for timber piles.

sections.title: Splices
sections.summary: Timber pile splices are undesirable: full bending strength is virtually impossible to develop; AASHTO (2010) allows them only if specified or approved in writing; order longer piles or redesign with more piles instead.
sections.body: 16.1.3 Splices (p. 397). Splices in timber piles are undesirable since developing the full bending strength of a spliced timber pile is virtually impossible. AASHTO (2010) states timber piles should not be spliced unless specified in the contract documents or approved in writing by the engineer. If lengths prove insufficient, order longer piles or redesign with additional piles of the furnished length.
key_points: Timber pile splices are undesirable (full bending strength not achievable)
Order longer piles or add piles instead of splicing
sections.applicability: Splicing timber piles.

sections.title: Steel H-Piles
sections.summary: H-piles penetrate hard or problematic upper layers to very dense or hard bearing layers such as rock, often needing splices and sometimes toe attachments; see 16.2.1 (toe attachments), 16.2.2 (splices) and 16.5 (welding).
sections.body: 16.2 Steel H-Piles (p. 398). Steel H-piles often penetrate hard or problematic upper layers to terminate in a very dense or hard bearing layer such as rock, at depths that may need single or multiple splices; toe attachments may be needed to prevent or reduce toe damage depending on surficial materials. Toe attachments are in 16.2.1, splicing in 16.2.2, welding procedures and inspection in 16.5.
key_points: H-piles to hard bearing layers often need splices and toe attachments
Welding procedures and inspection matter (Section 16.5)
sections.applicability: Toe protection and splicing of steel H-piles.

sections.title: Pile Toe Attachments
sections.summary: Unprotected H-pile toes in fills, very dense gravel or boulders can deform and the flanges separate from the web; cast steel shoes (ASTM A148, Grade 90-60) fillet welded along the outside flanges (5/16 in. or more) protect them and spread contact stresses on hard or sloping rock; welded plate reinforcement is not recommended; shoes of similar material are equivalent.
sections.body: 16.2.1 Pile Toe Attachments (pp. 398 to 400). H-piles install easily as non-displacement piles, but in man-made fills, very dense gravel or boulders the toe may deform unacceptably and flanges separate from the web: Figure 16-4 shows an H-pile driven without a shoe through boulders, extracted after dynamic test records indicated toe damage, with a boulder wedged between the flanges and flange-web separation. Manufactured shoes minimize or prevent this and spread high local contact stresses on hard rock, particularly sloping rock. Steel plates welded to flanges and web are not recommended: they give neither protection nor strength at the critical flange-to-web connection. Shoes (Figure 16-5) should be cast steel to ASTM A148/A148M (Grade 90-60), attached with fillet welds along the outside of each flange (Figure 16-6); flanges are usually beveled and a 5/16 in. or larger fillet weld (by flange thickness) used, per the agency's standard detail. Shoes from different manufacturers should be considered equivalent if of similar strength and fabrication; minor configuration differences matter little except where a shape has a definite advantage.
key_points: Unprotected toes in fills, dense gravel or boulders deform; flanges separate from web
Shoes spread contact stresses on hard and sloping rock
Welded plate toe reinforcement not recommended (no strength at flange-web connection)
Cast steel shoes ASTM A148 (Grade 90-60), 5/16 in. or larger fillet welds on outside flanges
Shoes of similar material and fabrication are equivalent

figures.title: Damaged H-pile driven without pile toe protection
Styles of H-pile driving shoes

sections.applicability: Toe protection for steel H-piles.

sections.title: Splices
sections.summary: H-pile splices: full penetration groove welds on web and flanges, or manufactured splicers (5/16 in. fillet welds 2.5 to 4 in. long at the corners, add-on flanges chamfered 45 deg, then full or partial groove welds); splices must meet compression, tension and bending demands; certified welders; splicers of the same steel as the pile (usually A572 Grade 50 or higher).
sections.body: 16.2.2 Splices (pp. 400 to 403). Splices are routinely full penetration groove welds along web and both flanges (Figure 16-7) or manufactured splicers (Figure 16-8); some agencies add welded square or diamond backer plates. Splices must satisfy all axial compression, tension and bending demands, which govern the choice; weld strength beyond driving needs is required for bending and cyclic loads, so certified welders and approved procedures are essential (16.5). With a manufactured splicer a notch is cut in the driven pile's web, the splicer slipped over, and 5/16 in. fillet welds about 2.5 to 4 in. long made vertically from its four corners to the flanges; the add-on section's flanges are chamfered 45 deg, the section aligned and held, the same 5/16 in. fillet welds made to its flanges, then full or partial penetration groove welds (by design) along both flanges (Figure 16-9). Most H-piles are ASTM A572 Grade 50 or higher; splicers should be the same steel.
key_points: Full penetration groove welds on web and flanges, or manufactured splicers
Splices must meet axial compression, tension and bending demands
Splicer: 5/16 in. fillet welds 2.5 to 4 in. long; add-on flanges chamfered 45 deg
Certified welders; splicers of the same high strength steel as the pile

sections.title: Steel Pipe Piles
sections.summary: Pipe piles are driven closed or open end, with toe attachments for both to limit toe damage and deflection; lengths are easily extended by welded or friction splices (16.3.1, 16.3.2; welding in 16.5).
sections.body: 16.3 Steel Pipe Piles (p. 403). Steel pipe piles may be driven closed or open end, and toe attachments exist for both to minimize toe damage in difficult conditions and limit deflection; lengths are easily increased in the field by welded or friction splices. Toe attachments are in 16.3.1, splices in 16.3.2, welding in 16.5.
key_points: Toe attachments for closed and open end pipe piles limit damage and deflection
Lengths extended by welded or friction splices
sections.applicability: Toe attachments, splices and constrictor plates for steel pipe piles.

sections.title: Pile Toe Attachments
sections.summary: Closed end pipes: flat closure plates 0.75 to 1.0 in. thick for 18 in. or smaller (thicker for larger), 5/8 in. larger than the pipe for a 5/16 in. fillet weld, A36 or better; conical tips (rounded or 60 deg, A148 cast) cost more and may drive slightly longer; 'rock crusher' shoes for sloping rock. Open end pipes: inside or outside flange cutting shoes (A148); 36 in. and larger use a thicker wall over the lower two diameters.
sections.body: 16.3.1 Pile Toe Attachments (pp. 403 to 408). Toe attachments reduce toe damage and limit deflection: closed end pipes may deflect at obstructions, and open end toes may deform in very dense materials. Closed end pipes most often have a flat plate welded to the toe (Figure 16-10), 0.75 to 1.0 in. thick for outside diameters of 18 in. or less (thicker for larger piles), typically 5/8 in. larger in diameter than the pipe to allow a 5/16 in. fillet weld, or the same diameter with a beveled partial penetration weld; ASTM A36 or better. Conical toe attachments, rounded or with a 60 degree point (Figures 16-11, 16-12), cost more; flat plates develop higher unit toe resistance, so a conical tip may drive slightly longer for the same resistance; they are full or partial penetration groove welded and cast to ASTM A148 (Grade 90-60). A 'rock crusher' shoe, a thick flat plate with heavy plates forming a 45 degree point, is preferred where sloping bedrock is met (Figure 16-13). Open end pipes in dense gravel or to rock use cast steel (A148 Grade 90-60) cutting shoes, inside or outside flange (Figure 16-14), each with a bearing ring; outside flanges ease drilling through the toe but their larger perimeter can reduce shaft resistance, and are sometimes friction fit only (Figures 16-15, 16-16). For open end pipes 36 in. or larger in heavily loaded foundations with few piles, a thicker wall over the lower two diameters, with the same outside diameter, is preferred, acting as an inside cutting shoe against boulders, sloping bedrock or batter installation.
key_points: Closure plates 0.75 to 1.0 in. for <= 18 in. pipes; 5/8 in. oversize for 5/16 in. fillet weld; A36
Conical tips (rounded or 60 deg) cost more; flat plates give higher unit toe resistance
'Rock crusher' shoe preferred on sloping bedrock
Open end cutting shoes, inside or outside flange (outside flange may reduce shaft resistance)
Open pipes >= 36 in.: thicker wall over the lower two diameters

sections.title: Splices
sections.summary: Pipe pile splices: full penetration welds with backing rings (pins give the root gap), preferred where full bending strength is needed; or drive-fit friction splicers (A27 or A148 cast, tapered, 3/8 in. bearing at mid-height) needing square ends, fillet welded for full bending strength (fully seated first), uplift checked, welds on spiral pipe against leakage.
sections.body: 16.3.2 Splices (pp. 408 to 412). Pipe sections are spliced by full penetration welding (Figure 16-17(a)) or a mechanical drive-fit friction splicer (Figure 16-17(b)). Where full bending strength is needed a friction splicer needs fillet welds, made only after it is fully seated in both sections to avoid weld cracking, so full penetration welds are preferred. A backing ring (Figure 16-18) sits between the sections and aids alignment, its pins giving a gap for the root pass (Figure 16-19); further passes complete the weld (Figure 16-20). Drive-fit splicers (Figures 16-21, 16-22) are cast from ASTM A27 (Grade 65-35) or A148/A148M (Grade 90-60) with a taper for a friction connection without welding and a 3/8 in. bearing at mid-height for load transfer; adjoining ends must be square (a damaged driven top cut off square). Without fillet welds top and bottom they do not give full bending strength; their suitability for uplift is for the designer; on spiral welded pipe fillet welds are often needed against groundwater leakage.
key_points: Full penetration weld with backing ring preferred for full bending strength
Friction splicer fillet welds only after full seating, to avoid cracking
Drive-fit splicers: cast A27 or A148, tapered, 3/8 in. bearing; ends must be square
Designer checks friction splicers under uplift; weld on spiral pipe against leakage

sections.title: Constrictor Plates
sections.summary: Large diameter open end pipe (LDOEP) piles can core during driving; a constrictor plate welded inside at a target depth forces plugging and a larger nominal resistance; research is ongoing.
sections.body: 16.3.3 Constrictor Plates (p. 413). As discussed in Section 6.4.2 and 'Section 7.10 7' (as printed), LDOEP piles can 'core' or remain unplugged during driving; a constrictor plate designed and welded inside the pile promotes plugging at a targeted depth in the stratigraphy. Figure 16-23 shows the top of a constrictor plate with stiffeners inside a 60 in. O.D. pipe; another detail is Figure 6-14. Constrictor plates force plugged behavior and larger nominal resistance; research on LDOEP design including them is ongoing.
key_points: LDOEP piles can core (remain unplugged) during driving
Constrictor plate inside the pile forces plugging at a target depth

sections.title: Precast Concrete Piles
sections.summary: Heading for precast concrete pile accessories: toe attachments (16.4.1) and splices (16.4.2).
sections.body: 16.4 Precast Concrete Piles (p. 414). The heading is followed directly by 16.4.1 (Pile Toe Attachment) and then 16.4.2 (Splices).
key_points: Precast concrete pile toe attachments (16.4.1) and splices (16.4.2)
sections.applicability: Toe attachments and splice selection for precast prestressed concrete piles.

sections.title: Pile Toe Attachment
sections.summary: Concrete pile toes can be damaged in hard driving; when needed, flat cast steel shoes or Oslo / Rock Injector points (3.5 in. hardened steel point) are cast in, never field attached; H-pile or pipe sections cast into the toe aid penetration of very dense or hard materials and must be sized to avoid overstress.
sections.body: 16.4.1 Pile Toe Attachment (pp. 414 to 415). Concrete pile toes may be damaged in compression in hard driving; for hard driving and toe bearing on rock, cast steel attachments can be added during casting, though not routinely. A flat cast steel shoe (Figure 16-24(a)) or an 'Oslo Point' or 'Rock Injector Point' (Figure 16-24(b)) lets the pile be 'chiseled into' most rock for seating, generally with a 3.5 in. diameter hardened steel point in a steel casting (Figure 16-25). All toe attachments for precast concrete piles must be attached during casting, not in the field. An H-pile or pipe section cast into the toe of a prestressed pile (Figure 16-26) is used less for protection than to reach penetration depths in very dense or hard materials difficult for a displacement pile, with or without its own toe protection, and must be sized for the concrete section, loads and subsurface conditions to prevent overstressing.
key_points: Concrete pile toe attachments are cast in, never field attached
Oslo / Rock Injector points: 3.5 in. hardened steel point for seating in rock
Embedded H-pile or pipe stingers aid penetration; size to prevent overstressing

sections.title: Splices
sections.summary: Prestressed pile ends are not fully prestressed, so avoid splices by ordering length. Splice types: dowel, welded, mechanical, sleeve (Figure 16-27); Table 16-1 (Mullins and Sen 2015) rates capacity, failure type, durability, installation and U.S. production. Epoxy dowel splices are cheap but slow and limited in flexure and tension; mechanical splices handle tension; sleeves cut tension driving stresses but not for uplift.
sections.body: 16.4.2 Splices (pp. 416 to 421). Virtually all U.S. concrete piles are prestressed, but ends are not effectively prestressed within the development length, so splicing needs care; order sufficient length where possible. Splices are dowel, welded, mechanical or sleeve (Figure 16-27; wedge and pinned connectors mechanical, connector ring a sleeve). Table 16-1 (Mullins and Sen 2015; name, type: capacity, failure, durability, installation, U.S. produced): Epoxy Dowel, dowel: poor, ductile, good, moderate/poor, yes; Kie-Lock, mechanical: good, ductile, moderate, good, no; ICP, welded: good, brittle, moderate, moderate, no; NU Chuck, bolted: good, brittle, moderate, untested/moderate, yes; UF Tube, grouted tube: good, ductile, good, poor, yes (voided piles); GYA, mechanical: good, ductile, moderate, good, no; Macalloy, post-tensioned: good, ductile, good, moderate/poor, no. Capacity is meeting flexural and tensile requirements; ductile failure is preferred; durability is corrosion resistance; foreign splices need exceptions on some Federal projects. Epoxy dowel (Figures 16-28, 16-29): holes cast or drilled in the bottom section, dowels cast in the top section, a sheet metal form and poured epoxy; driving resumes after one to two days; slow but inexpensive and reliable with adequate dowels and epoxy, but limited in flexure and tension. Welded splices need steel fittings cast in, welded around the perimeter (ICP, Figure 16-30). Mechanical splices (Kie-Lock, Herkules/Hercules, ABB) are steel castings in the forms, locked by bars, wedges, pins or keys; expensive but fast and designed for all loads including tension (Figure 16-31). A post-tensioned splice under FDOT development restores full prestress across the joint (Figure 16-32). Sleeve splices (Hawaiian can, Bruns connector ring; Figure 16-33) are rapid and reduce tension driving stresses but not for static uplift; the short Bruns ring has limited tensile and flexural strength. Substitutes for a specified splice need equivalent compressive, tensile and flexural strength and field testing on spliced test piles.
key_points: Prestressed pile ends are not fully prestressed: order length to avoid splices
Splice types: dowel, welded, mechanical, sleeve (Table 16-1 ratings)
Epoxy dowel: inexpensive but slow; limited flexural and tensile strength
Mechanical splices: costly, fast, designed for tension
Sleeve splices reduce tension driving stresses but not for static uplift
Substitute splices need equivalent strength and field testing

sections.title: Welded Splices and Toe Attachments
sections.summary: Field weld quality governs splice and toe attachment strength (Michigan DOT Field Manual for Pile Welding 2012; NYSDOT 2012); welds crack or break from bending during misalignment or welding in the cold without preheat; causes are poor surface preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, or non-compliance with procedures.
sections.body: 16.5 Welded Splices and Toe Attachments (pp. 422 to 423). Field welding is needed on many splices and toe attachments, and weld quality maintains full pile strength; Michigan DOT's 'Field Manual for Pile Welding' (2012) and NYSDOT's 'Pile Driving Inspection Manual' (2012, with minimum splice times by section and splice type) address it. Improper welds crack or break in driving: a pipe weld cracked from bending during hammer-pile misalignment (Figure 16-34); an H-pile splice made in low temperatures without preheat broke a few blows after splicing (Figure 16-35). Main causes are poor surface preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, or non-compliance with approved procedures or details.
key_points: Weld quality governs splice and toe attachment strength
Failures: bending from misalignment; welding in the cold without preheat
Causes: poor preparation, insufficient bevel or root opening, non-compliance

Broken weld on H-pile splice

sections.applicability: Field welding of pile splices and toe attachments, and its inspection.

sections.title: Welding Surface Preparation
sections.summary: Clean the joint, preheat below 32 F, bevel for full penetration (H-pile add-on 45 deg bevel with 1/8 or 1/4 in. root opening); check alignment and root opening before welding, especially with H-pile splicers; a poorly welded splice separated and lost the lower pile.
sections.body: 16.5.1 Welding Surface Preparation (pp. 423 to 426). Clean the joint before welding and preheat below 32 degrees F. Pipe heads must be cut and beveled at the required angle (Figure 16-36), or penetration is reduced and a full penetration groove weld impossible; grinding prepares the surface (Figure 16-37). The add-on H-pile section typically has a 45 degree bevel with a 1/8 or 1/4 in. root opening; Figure 16-38 shows sections with no root opening or bevel, making the specified full penetration weld impossible. Align sections before splicing: Figure 16-39 shows misalignment, a poor groove weld and short, poor fillet welds with a splicer; check alignment and root opening first. Figure 16-40: on the same project dynamic testing indicated a cracked weld, and on extraction only the upper section returned, the splicer and lower section lost below ground.
key_points: Clean the joint; preheat below 32 F
Bevel for full penetration; H-pile add-on 45 deg bevel, 1/8 or 1/4 in. root opening
Check section alignment and root opening before welding

sections.title: Temperature Requirements During Welding and Splicing
sections.summary: Below 32 F ambient, preheat the steel within 3 in. of the weld to at least 70 F immediately before welding and keep it at least 50 F until complete; no welding below 0 F.
sections.body: 16.5.2 Temperature Requirements During Welding and Splicing (pp. 426 to 427). Where ambient air is below 32 degrees F, preheat the steel near the splice to at least 70 degrees F within 3 in. of the weld immediately before welding and maintain at least 50 degrees F until welding is complete; do not weld below 0 degrees F ambient (Figure 16-41, preheating an H-pile splice). (The 16.5.4.1 checklist says the area is 'maintained at 70 degrees'.)
key_points: Below 32 F: preheat to >= 70 F within 3 in. of the weld
Maintain >= 50 F until welding is complete
No welding below 0 F ambient

figures.title: Heating pile splice location prior to welding

sections.applicability: Cold weather welding of pile splices.

sections.title: Welding Pile Toe Accessories
sections.summary: Weld toe attachments by approved procedures and welders; small spot welds can lose the shoe in hard driving; a partial penetration groove weld along the full flange length greatly reduces shoe loss on cobbles or bedrock.
sections.body: 16.5.3 Welding Pile Toe Accessories (pp. 427 to 428). Toe attachments on H-piles and pipe piles should be welded by approved welders to the approved procedure. Small spot welds (one on the web, one at each flange corner; Figure 16-42) can let the shoe be lost in difficult driving; a partial penetration groove weld along the full length of the flange (Figure 16-43) greatly reduces the chance of shoe loss or malfunction on cobbles or bedrock.
key_points: Approved welders and procedures for toe attachments
Spot welds are unsatisfactory: the shoe can be lost
Full-length partial penetration groove weld on the flanges

sections.title: Welded Splice Checklist
sections.summary: The welded splice checklist from the Michigan DOT Field Manual for Pile Welding (2012) covers preparation (16.5.4.1), welding (16.5.4.2) and final inspection (16.5.4.3).
sections.body: 16.5.4 Welded Splice Checklist (p. 429). The checklist is from the Michigan DOT Field Manual for Pile Welding (2012) and highlights key items for successful field welded splices, in three parts: preparation, during welding, and final weld inspection.
key_points: Michigan DOT (2012) checklist: preparation, during welding, final inspection
sections.applicability: Checklist for field welded pile splices.

sections.title: Preparation
sections.summary: Preparation: certified welders, an approved Weld Procedure Specification (WPS), joint preparation per plans, ground and clean surfaces, preheat below 32 F (maintained at 70 degrees as printed) and no welding below 0 F, and an approved quality control plan.
sections.body: 16.5.4.1 Preparation (p. 429). Welders certified by an authorized agency for the work and weld type; a Weld Procedure Specification (WPS) developed and approved before work; joint preparation, alignment, root openings, bevels and fit up per plans; weld surfaces ground and cleaned of coatings, oil, grease, rust, dirt, moisture and contaminants; below 32 degrees F ambient the splice area preheated and maintained at 70 degrees, no welding below 0 degrees F, heating and housing as approved; an approved contractor quality control plan followed.
key_points: Certified welders and an approved Weld Procedure Specification (WPS)
Joint preparation, alignment, bevels and root openings per plans
Clean weld zone; preheat below 32 F; no welding below 0 F
Approved contractor quality control plan
sections.applicability: Preparation items of the welded splice checklist.

sections.title: During Welding
sections.summary: During welding: store electrodes sealed or in a hot box at 250 F or more; use within two hours of exposure or redry two hours at 500 degrees or more; discard wet or dropped electrodes; tack welds not part of the final weld; follow the WPS; clean between passes; back gouge full penetration welds.
sections.body: 16.5.4.2 During Welding (p. 429). Electrodes stored in a hermetically sealed container or hot box at a minimum of 250 degrees F; once exposed used within two hours or redried two hours at a minimum of 500 degrees; wet electrodes discarded, as are those dropped, rained on or improperly stored. Tack welds used in fit up not part of the final weld; welders follow the approved WPS and quality control plan and inspect their own work, clean slag and repair discontinuities between passes, and back gouge to sound metal before welding the backside of full penetration groove welds.
key_points: Electrodes sealed or in a hot box at >= 250 F
Exposed electrodes used within 2 hours or redried 2 hours at >= 500 degrees
Discard wet, dropped or improperly stored electrodes
Clean between passes; back gouge full penetration groove welds
sections.applicability: Welding items of the welded splice checklist.

sections.title: Final Weld Inspection
sections.summary: Final inspection: remove slag, spatter and debris; check size, length and profile; grind arc strikes; inspect for cracks, porosity, undercut, underfill, overlap, lack of penetration or fusion; repair before acceptance.
sections.body: 16.5.4.3 Final Weld Inspection (p. 430). Remove all slag, spatter and debris from the weld surface; weld size, length and profile meet requirements; arc strikes ground smooth; a final inspection for cracks or other discontinuities, porosity, undercut, underfill, overlap, lack of penetration or lack of fusion before acceptance; repairs or replacement made before accepting the weld.
key_points: Remove slag, spatter and debris; grind arc strikes
Check weld size, length and profile
Inspect for cracks, porosity, undercut, underfill, overlap, lack of penetration or fusion
sections.applicability: Final inspection items of the welded splice checklist.
